q: Which bear, famous for its black-and-white fur and its diet of bamboo, lives in the wild only in the mountain forests of China?
explain: The giant panda eats almost nothing but bamboo and lives in misty mountain forests in central China.

q: Which river of northern China, called the cradle of Chinese civilisation, carries so much yellow silt that it is named after its colour?
explain: The Yellow River, or Huang He, picks up golden silt from the loess plateau, which gives the water its colour and the river its name.

q: Which buried army of thousands of life-size terracotta soldiers, made to guard China's first emperor in the afterlife, was discovered by farmers near Xi'an in 1974?
explain: The Terracotta Army, with more than 8,000 soldiers, horses, and chariots, was buried with Emperor Qin Shi Huang over 2,000 years ago.

q: Which city on China's east coast, famous for its futuristic skyline and the historic Bund waterfront, stands near the mouth of the Yangtze?
explain: Shanghai, near where the Yangtze meets the sea, grew from a small fishing town into one of the world's great port cities.

q: Which board game, invented in China more than 2,000 years ago, is played on a grid of 361 intersections with black and white stones?
explain: Go, called Weiqi in Chinese, is one of the oldest board games in the world and is still played by millions of people.

q: Mount Everest, the highest peak in the world, stands on the border of China and Nepal — what is its Tibetan name?
explain: Qomolangma, which means Goddess Mother of the World in Tibetan, is the name local people have long used for Mount Everest.

q: The Three Gorges Dam, the world's largest hydroelectric power station, spans which great river in central China?
explain: The Three Gorges Dam crosses the Yangtze River in Hubei province, holding back a huge reservoir and generating enormous amounts of electricity.

q: Which Hindu festival of lights, celebrated across India every autumn with oil lamps, candles, and fireworks, marks the victory of light over darkness?
explain: Diwali is one of India's biggest and brightest celebrations, with lamps glowing in windows and streets all over the country.

q: Which big cat, with orange fur and black stripes, is India's national animal and prowls forests and grasslands across the country?
explain: The Bengal tiger, India's national animal, is protected in national parks and reserves across the country.

q: Which Indian stringed instrument, with a long neck and a round gourd body, is famous in Indian classical music?
explain: The sitar, with its long neck and shimmering strings, creates the sliding, singing sounds heard in Indian classical music.

q: Which hilltop fort near Jaipur in Rajasthan, built from red sandstone and pale marble, is famous for its glittering hall of mirrors?
explain: The Amber Fort, also called Amer Fort, overlooks Jaipur and its Sheesh Mahal hall is covered inside with tiny mirrors.

q: Which river rises in the Western Ghats of Karnataka, flows east across southern India, and empties into the Bay of Bengal in Tamil Nadu?
explain: The Kaveri, also spelled Cauvery, flows for roughly 800 kilometres, watering farmland across Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.

q: Which state in India's far northeast is famous for its tea gardens on the Brahmaputra plains and for Kaziranga National Park, home of the one-horned rhinoceros?
explain: Assam's Kaziranga National Park is one of the last strongholds of the one-horned rhinoceros, and the state's hills grow some of India's finest tea.

q: Which peak in the Indian Himalaya of Uttarakhand is the highest mountain located entirely within India?
explain: Nanda Devi, at 7,816 metres, is the highest peak wholly inside India; Kangchenjunga, though higher, stands on the border with Nepal.

q: Which Japanese dish of vinegared rice topped or wrapped with raw fish has become a favourite food all over the world?
explain: Sushi, vinegared rice paired with raw fish or other toppings, is now eaten in almost every country on Earth.

q: What is the name of Japan's famous high-speed train, nicknamed the bullet train, which has raced between cities since 1964?
explain: The Shinkansen, or bullet train, was the world's first high-speed rail service and still carries millions of passengers every day.

q: Which pavilion in Kyoto, covered in gold leaf and reflecting in a pond, is one of Japan's most photographed landmarks?
explain: Kinkaku-ji, the Golden Pavilion, was built in the 1300s and its top two floors are covered in gold leaf.

q: Which Japanese company, founded in Kyoto in 1889 as a playing-card maker, now makes the Switch console and Mario games?
explain: Nintendo began by making hanafuda playing cards in 1889 and grew into one of the world's most famous video game companies.

q: Which warm ocean current, one of the strongest in the world, sweeps northeast along Japan's southern Pacific coast?
explain: The Kuroshio, or Japan Current, carries warm tropical water north along Japan's east coast, shaping its climate and rich fisheries.

q: Which island, the northernmost of Japan's four main islands, is famous for its ski resorts, hot springs, and the Snow Festival in Sapporo?
explain: Hokkaido, Japan's second-largest island, lies north of Honshu and is loved for its powder snow and wide-open spaces.

q: Which traditional Japanese theatre, performed by male actors, is famous for its dramatic face paint, stylised poses, and stories of samurai and merchants?
explain: Kabuki actors wear bold kumadori makeup and strike mie poses to tell tales of heroes, villains, and everyday life.

q: Which spicy Korean side dish of fermented vegetables, usually napa cabbage and radish with chilli and garlic, is served at almost every meal?
explain: Kimchi is Korea's national dish, with hundreds of recipes, and many families keep a special fridge just for fermenting it.

q: What is the name of the Korean pop music phenomenon, with catchy songs, colourful videos, and devoted fan clubs, that has swept the world since the 2000s?
explain: K-pop, short for Korean pop, has become a worldwide craze with its catchy songs and high-energy dance routines.

q: Which grand palace in Seoul, with its colourful throne hall and changing-of-the-guard ceremony, was the main royal palace of Korea's Joseon kings?
explain: Gyeongbokgung, built in 1395, was the largest and most important of Seoul's five grand palaces.

q: Which Korean martial art, whose name means the way of the hand and the foot, is practised by millions of people worldwide and became an Olympic sport in 2000?
explain: Taekwondo, known for its high, fast kicks, became a full Olympic medal sport at the Sydney Games in 2000.

q: Which country shares South Korea's only land border, across the heavily fortified Korean Demilitarized Zone?
explain: The Korean Peninsula's only land border is between North and South Korea, marked by the 250-kilometre-long DMZ.

q: Which river forms part of the boundary between North Korea and China before flowing southwest into the Yellow Sea?
explain: The Yalu River, about 800 kilometres long, separates North Korea from China's Liaoning province for much of its course.

q: Which Indonesian island, famous for its Hindu temples, terraced rice fields, and beach resorts, welcomes millions of holidaymakers every year?
explain: Bali, the Island of the Gods, is Indonesia's most famous holiday island, known for its temples, rice terraces, and surf beaches.

q: Which giant lizard, the largest living lizard on Earth, is found in the wild only on Komodo and a few nearby islands of Indonesia?
explain: The Komodo dragon can grow over three metres long and lives in the wild only on a handful of Indonesian islands.

q: Which Indonesian dish of fried rice, seasoned with sweet soy sauce and shallots and often topped with a fried egg, is a national favourite?
explain: Nasi goreng, which simply means fried rice in Indonesian, is cooked in almost every home and street stall across the country.

q: Borneo, the world's third-largest island, is shared by Indonesia, Malaysia, and which tiny sultanate on its northern coast?
explain: Brunei, a small sultanate, occupies two stretches of Borneo's northern coast, while Malaysia and Indonesia share the rest of the island.

q: Which ancient temple in central Java, built around 800 AD with hundreds of Buddha statues and stupas, is the world's largest Buddhist temple?
explain: Borobudur, on the island of Java, was buried under volcanic ash for centuries and is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

q: Which strait separates the Indonesian islands of Sumatra and Java, and is overlooked by the Krakatoa volcano group?
explain: The Sunda Strait lies between Java and Sumatra, and the Krakatoa volcanoes rise from its waters.

q: Which animal, with its long trunk and tusks, is a sacred symbol of Thailand and once helped people carry logs through the forests?
explain: The Asian elephant is Thailand's national animal and a sacred symbol, and many now live in ethical sanctuaries.

q: Which Thai noodle dish, stir-fried with tamarind, peanuts, bean sprouts, and lime, is one of the world's most famous street foods?
explain: Pad thai is the stir-fried noodle dish you will find on Thai street corners everywhere, topped with crushed peanuts and lime.

q: Which dazzling white temple in Chiang Rai, decorated with mirrors and glass, was designed and built by a contemporary Thai artist?
options: The Temple of the Reclining Buddha
explain: Wat Rong Khun, the White Temple, is the life's work of Thai artist Chalermchai Kositpipat and is still being built.

q: Which river, called the River of Kings, flows through the heart of Bangkok and has shaped Thai life, trade, and farming for centuries?
explain: The Chao Phraya runs through central Thailand past Bangkok and into the Gulf of Thailand, watering the country's rice farms.

q: Which narrow strip of land, the slimmest part of the Malay Peninsula, connects mainland Asia to the peninsula and has long been discussed as a site for a canal?
explain: The Kra Isthmus, in southern Thailand, is only about 44 kilometres wide at its narrowest point.

q: Which classical Thai dance, with glittering costumes, elegant hand gestures, and masked performers, tells stories from the Ramakien, the Thai version of the Ramayana?
explain: Khon is Thailand's classical masked dance, traditionally performed by men, with every gesture following strict rules.

q: Which Vietnamese noodle soup, with fragrant broth, rice noodles, fresh herbs, and slices of beef or chicken, is eaten for breakfast all over Vietnam?
explain: Pho, pronounced fuh, is Vietnam's most famous dish, and a hot bowl of it is a typical Vietnamese breakfast.

q: Which bay in northern Vietnam, dotted with thousands of limestone islands and islets rising from green water, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
explain: Ha Long Bay, whose name means where the dragon descends to the sea, is famous for its towering limestone karsts.

q: Which traditional Vietnamese dress, a long close-fitting silk tunic worn over trousers, is worn at weddings, graduations, and the Lunar New Year?
explain: The áo dài, with its high collar and flowing panels, is the traditional dress of Vietnam, often worn on special occasions.

q: Which city in central Vietnam, on the Perfume River, was the imperial capital of the Nguyen emperors and is famous for its ancient citadel?
explain: Huế, on the Perfume River, was Vietnam's imperial capital, and its Citadel is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

q: Which mountain range, also called the Truong Son, runs along the border between Vietnam and Laos?
explain: The Annamite Range, or Truong Son, forms much of the long border between Vietnam and Laos, with dense forests and rare wildlife.

q: Which city in southern Vietnam, on the Saigon River, is the country's largest and was formerly known as Saigon?
explain: Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam's biggest city, was called Saigon until it was renamed in 1976.
